extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis and Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Verify/apply singularity structure and curvature-estimate results for Ricci flow on compact orientable three-manifolds with normalized initial metrics; identify canonical neighborhoods and perform rescaling limits to ancient κ-solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized metric condition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Riemannian metric on a compact orientable three-manifold is called normalized if the eigenvalues of its curvature operator at every point are bounded by 1/10, and every geodesic ball of radius one has volume at least one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normalization is used so by rescaling one can ensure pinching estimates and κ-noncollapsing for limit solutions; any argument that invokes the pinching estimate assumes the initial metric is normalized (or is rescaled to be so).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamilton–Ivey pinching estimate (7.1.1)/(7.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The curvature satisfies the pinching estimate (7.1.1): Rm(x,t) ≥ −[f^{-1}(R(x,t)(1+t))/(R(x,t)(1+t))] R(x,t) on M × [0,T), equivalently rewritten as (7.1.2) in terms of the inverse function f^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This estimate controls negative eigenvalues ν relative to the scalar curvature R and is a basic input to obtain nonnegativity in limits and to apply canonical neighborhood conclusions. The precise functional form (and the function ω referenced elsewhere) is used in local curvature control and scaling arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Each point in an (ancient) κ-solution has a neighborhood which is either an evolving ε-neck, or an evolving ε-cap, or a compact (without boundary) positively curved manifold (metric quotient of round S^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principal classification used to describe high-curvature regions: when applying it one must check the ε-scale and the parabolic region; the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6 referenced) also provides radii r with Bt(x,r) ⊂ Bt(x,2r) and curvature bounds between (C2R)^{-1} and C2R on such neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume estimate for neck/cap neighborhoods (cases (a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases (a) and (b) (neck or cap neighborhoods) the neighborhood B is required to satisfy the volume estimate 1/(C2 R(x,t))^{3/2} Vol_t(B) ≤ ε r^3 (as stated in the text in the context of cases (a) and (b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking whether a given neighborhood falls into case (a) or (b) one must verify not only the geometric shape (ε-neck or ε-cap) but also this small-volume condition relative to the local curvature scale; the constants C2 and the allowed ε are singled out in the canonical neighborhood statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsing on all scales
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution (or limit solution) is κ-noncollapsed on all scales (for some κ>0 or universal κ0), i.e. lower bounds on volume relative to curvature on balls at all scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perelman's no local collapsing theorems I and II are used to obtain uniform injectivity radius/volume lower bounds in rescaling limits. Many compactness and convergence results require verifying κ-noncollapsedness on the relevant scales (sometimes depending only on T0 or A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity structure theorem (Theorem 7.1.1) — ε-closeness to ancient κ-solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 and T0>1 there exists r0>0 such that: if g_{ij}(x,t) is a solution on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric and t0 ≥ 1, and if Q = R(x0,t0) ≥ r0^{-2}, then the solution in the parabolic region { (x,t) | t0 − d^2_{t0}(x,x0) < ε^{-2} Q^{-1}, t0 − (1/2)Q^{-1} ≤ t ≤ t0 } is, after scaling by factor Q, ε-close in the C[ε^{-1}]-topology to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient κ-solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the precise criterion to detect canonical neighborhood structure near high-curvature points by rescaling: you must check the parabolic space-time region and the scalar curvature scale Q, and closeness is measured in the C^{[ε^{-1}]} topology to an orientable ancient κ-solution (for some κ>0).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescaling at almost-maximum points yields ancient κ-solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If one takes a sequence of almost-maximum curvature points (pk, tk) with appropriate scaling factors Qk = R(pk,tk) and applies Hamilton's compactness theorem together with Perelman's no local collapsing, then a subsequence of the scalings converges in C^∞_loc to a nonflat complete orientable ancient κ-solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural criterion is used repeatedly: identify almost-maximal curvature points, rescale by their scalar curvature, and check κ-noncollapsedness and pinching estimates to extract ancient κ-solution limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic-type curvature estimate (Theorem 7.2.1) — hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: For any A<∞ there exist K=K(A) and α=α(A)>0 such that: if a solution on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric is defined for 0 ≤ t ≤ r0^2 (with r0<α), satisfies |Rm(x,t)| ≤ 2 r0^{-2} for 0 ≤ t ≤ r0^2 and d0(x,x0) ≤ r0, and Vol_0(B_0(x0,r0)) ≥ A^{-1} r0^3, then the conclusion below holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem requires uniform curvature bound on the parabolic neighborhood, a small scale r0 (bounded by α), and a lower volume bound at time 0; these are the precise preconditions to infer the curvature control conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic-type curvature estimate (Theorem 7.2.1) — conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses, R(x,r0^2) ≤ K r0^{-2} whenever d^2_{r0}(x,x0) < A r0 (i.e. for spatial points within A r0 at the scaled time r0^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an a priori curvature upper bound at time r0^2 in a spatial region depending on A, given the initial volume lower bound and parabolic curvature control; constants K and α depend on A (and are obtained via the compactness/rescaling/contradiction argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point adjustment / maximality selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving contradiction-based curvature estimates, choose points (xk,tk) so that the desired conclusion fails at (xk,tk) but holds for any earlier point (x,t) with R(x,t) > 2 R(xk,tk) in a prescribed backward time interval; this process terminates in finitely many steps because the solution is smooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selection yields a point that is suitably maximal in curvature growth properties and is essential to set up the rescaling limit; one must check the backward parabolic neighborhoods and use Li–Yau–Hamilton and pinching estimates to control the evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature derivative bounds (Lemma 7.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a small universal c>0, for points (x̄, t̄) with t̄ in a short backward interval and d_{t̄}(x, x̄) ≤ (c � Q̄^{-1/2}) (with Q̄ = Q + R(x̄,t̄)), one has R_k(x,t) ≤ 4 R_k(x̄,t̄) on that backward parabolic neighborhood (the lemma gives a local curvature bound by integrating derivative estimates from ancient κ-solutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma provides the local curvature control needed to apply Hamilton's compactness theorem and Shi's derivative estimates; its proof uses derivative estimates |∇R| and |∂R/∂t| derived from closeness to an ancient κ-solution and integrates along space-time curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity/LI-Yau–Hamilton estimate usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Scalar curvature of (ancient) κ-solutions is pointwise nondecreasing in time; the Li–Yau–Hamilton inequality provides control of curvature ratios backward in time and comparability of distances at different times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this monotonicity to bound scalar curvature at earlier times (and to deduce control when extending limits backward in time). It is explicitly invoked to show nondecreasing infimum of scalar curvature and to compare metrics at different times (estimates like (7.1.3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alexandrov tangent-cone and splitting argument to rule out noncompact singular cones
rubrics_metrics.description: If a limiting local region U has nonnegative sectional curvature and a nonflat tangent cone at a boundary point y (in the Alexandrov sense), then taking further blow-ups and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and splitting arguments leads to contradictions (nonflat cone would locally split off radial directions Ricci-flatly), so such configurations are ruled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This geometric analysis criterion is used to show that curvature of rescaled limits cannot blow up at finite distance from basepoints; one must check nonnegativity in Alexandrov sense and then apply cone-splitting/splitting theorems to obtain the contradiction.
